youtube.title: Decimals for Kids: Tenths on a Number Line | Grade 4 Math | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Turtle's race is 1.5 metres long, but Robo built a 15-metre track! What does that little dot mean?
Kids learn what a tenth is (1/10 = 0.1), how the decimal point separates wholes from tenths, how to read 1.5 as one and five tenths, how to place tenths on a number line and a metre stick, how to compare decimals (wholes first), and how to add and take away tenths with ten tenths making one whole.
Try at home: put a sticky note every 10 cm on a tape measure, roll a toy car and read where it stops as a decimal. Roll it on a clear floor away from stairs.

objects.text:
Tenths are 10 equal parts of a whole: 3/10 = 0.3.
The decimal point sits between wholes and tenths.
Compare the wholes first.
Ten tenths make one whole.
Tenths walk: put a sticky note every 10 cm on a tape, from 0.1 m to 1.0 m. Roll a toy car and read where it stops!

do.text: Tenths Track
Race day! My race is one point five metres long.
And I built the track! Fifteen metres! It goes right out the door!
Robo, look at the poster. What does this little dot mean?
Hmm. A dot? I thought it was a speck of chalk.
That dot is the decimal point. Let's find out what it does.
Here is one whole bar. Let's cut it into ten equal parts.
Each part is one tenth. Ten equal parts make the whole.
tenth
Shade one part. One tenth. We can write it as a fraction, or as a decimal.
Zero point one means zero wholes and one tenth.
0.1 = one tenth
Shade three parts. Three tenths. Zero point three.
All ten?
Shade all ten. Ten tenths make one whole. One point zero.
This is a place value chart. Ones on the left, tenths on the right.
The decimal point sits between the wholes and the tenths.
decimal point
So one point five is one whole, and five tenths!
1.5 = one and five tenths
We can read it two ways. One point five, or one and five tenths.
Let's practise. How do we read this one?
Two point seven. Two wholes and seven tenths!
2.7 = two and seven tenths
And this one? Zero wholes, and four tenths.
0.4 = four tenths
Back to one point five. Here is more evidence. Let's count every tenth.
15 tenths
Fifteen tenths! So one point five is also fifteen tenths.
But fifteen is one ten and five ones. That's ten times as far!
15 m is ten times 1.5 m
Oops. My track is ten times too long. I'll roll it up.
Fun fact: in France, Germany and Brazil, people write a comma instead of a point.
Here's the real track: zero to two metres. Every tenth gets a stepping stone.
Slow and steady. One tenth at a time!
Zero point nine. What comes after zero point nine?
Click! Ten tenths make one whole. One point zero.
Ten tenths make?
Ten tenths make?
One whole!
One point five! One whole and five tenths. I finished!
Now find some points. Zero point four!
Four tenths of a metre. On the metre stick, that's forty centimetres.
Each tenth of a metre is ten centimetres. Now, one point three!
One whole metre and three tenths. That's one hundred thirty centimetres.
And one point seven?
One and seven tenths. Easy!
Zero point nine beats one point two, because nine is bigger than two!
Is that true? Turtle, stand on each one.
Which is further?
One point two is further along. It's bigger.
Compare the wholes first. Zero point nine has no whole. One point two has one.
compare the wholes first
If the wholes are the same, then compare the tenths. One point four beats one point two.
then compare the tenths
Wholes first, then tenths. Got it!
Zero point six plus zero point three. Start at zero point six, and take three leaps.
Six tenths plus three tenths is nine tenths. Zero point nine.
Zero point seven plus zero point five. Seven plus five is twelve. So, zero point twelve!
Let's check on the track. Five leaps of one tenth.
We passed one whole! It's one point two, not zero point twelve.
Zero point twelve is even less than both numbers. That can't be the sum.
Let me write it in columns. Line up the decimal points, so tenths add to tenths.
Seven tenths plus five tenths is twelve tenths. That's one whole and two tenths.
12 tenths = 1.2
One point two. The point stays lined up.
Taking away works the same way. One point five take away zero point four.
Four leaps back. One point one.
Point one, point two, steady as I go!
Ten little tenths make a whole, you know!
Tiny steps for tenths, a big jump for a whole!
Point one, point two, steady as I go. Ten little tenths make a whole, you know!
Decimals are everywhere! Let's go on a decimal hunt.
This juice bottle holds one point five litres. One and five tenths litres.
This pencil is fourteen point five centimetres. Fourteen and five tenths.
Turtle's long jump: one point two metres. One and two tenths.
A thermometer reads thirty seven point zero degrees. That's normal body temperature!
Doctors measure it to a tenth of a degree.
Fun fact: in 1585, Simon Stevin wrote a little book to teach everyone decimals.
Challenge one! Put these in order, from least to greatest.
least to greatest
Zero point three, zero point eight, one point zero, one point four!
Wholes first: the zeros come first. Then the tenths decide.
Challenge two! Zero point four plus zero point eight?
Four tenths plus eight tenths is twelve tenths. One point two!
Challenge three! I walked zero point six metres, then zero point seven. How far?
Six tenths plus seven tenths is thirteen tenths. One point three metres!
Last one! Which ribbon is longer, one point one metres or zero point nine metres?
One point one. It has a whole metre, and zero point nine does not.
Quiz time! One: write seven tenths as a decimal.
Zero point seven.
Two: which is greater, one point two or zero point nine? Why?
One point two. It has one whole, and zero point nine has none.
Three: what is zero point eight plus zero point four?
Twelve tenths. One point two.
Four: how many centimetres is zero point three metres?
Three tenths of a metre is thirty centimetres.
Tenths are ten equal parts of a whole.
